## Proof

**Claim:** The only finite group with exactly two conjugacy classes is the cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$.

**Answer-leak check:** The problem statement contains no solution, answer value, or proof sketch. Proceeding.

---

**Proof.**

Let $G$ be a finite group with exactly two conjugacy classes. Since the identity $e$ is always in its own conjugacy class $\{e\}$ (as $geg^{-1}=e$), the second conjugacy class must be $G\setminus\{e\}$. Thus every non-identity element is conjugate to every other non-identity element.

Pick any $g\in G\setminus\{e\}$. Its conjugacy class is $G\setminus\{e\}$, which has size $|G|-1$.

By the orbit-stabilizer theorem (applied to the conjugation action of $G$ on itself), the size of the conjugacy class of $g$ equals the index of its centralizer:

$$|\mathrm{Cl}(g)| = [G : C_G(g)] = \frac{|G|}{|C_G(g)|}.$$

This quantity is a divisor of $|G|$. Therefore $|G|-1$ divides $|G|$.

Since $|G|-1$ divides both $|G|$ and $|G|-1$, it divides $\gcd(|G|,\,|G|-1)=1$. Hence $|G|-1=1$, so $|G|=2$.

A group of order $2$ is necessarily cyclic, $G\cong\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$. Its two conjugacy classes are $\{e\}$ and $\{g\}$, confirming it has exactly two conjugacy classes. $\blacksquare$

Let me think about this. A finite group with exactly two conjugacy classes. One conjugacy class is always {e} (the identity). So the other conjugacy class must be G \ {e}, meaning every non-identity element is conjugate to every other non-identity element.

This means all non-identity elements have the same order. Let me think about what groups have this property.

If all non-identity elements are conjugate, they all have the same order. Let the order of non-identity elements be p (must be prime, since if an element has order ab with a,b > 1, then its power has order a, but powers of conjugate elements... wait, conjugate elements have the same order, but powers of an element are not necessarily conjugate to it).

Actually, let me think more carefully. All non-identity elements are conjugate, so they all have the same order, say n. 

Since every non-identity element has order n, and the identity has order 1, the group has elements of orders 1 and n only.

If n is not prime, say n = ab with a, b > 1, then take any non-identity element g of order n. Then g^a has order b < n and g^a ≠ e, contradiction since g^a is a non-identity element with order b ≠ n. So n must be prime, say n = p.

So every non-identity element has order p. This means G is a group of exponent p (every element has order dividing p, and p is prime). 

For p = 2: every non-identity element has order 2, so G is an elementary abelian 2-group, i.e., G ≅ (Z/2Z)^k. But for this to have exactly two conjugacy classes, G must be abelian (which it is) and have exactly two elements, so |G| = 2, giving G ≅ Z/2Z.

Wait, if G is abelian, every element is its own conjugacy class. So G has exactly two conjugacy classes iff |G| = 2. So G ≅ Z/2Z.

For p odd: G has exponent p. If G is abelian, then again |G| = 2 which contradicts p odd. So G must be non-abelian. 

Non-abelian groups of exponent p exist for p ≥ 3. The smallest example is the Heisenberg group over F_p for p = 3, which has order 27 and exponent 3.

But wait, does the Heisenberg group over F_p have exactly two conjugacy classes? Let me check. The Heisenberg group over F_p is the group of 3×3 upper triangular matrices with 1s on the diagonal over F_p. It has order p^3. Its center has order p (the matrices with only the top-right entry nonzero). The conjugacy classes: the center elements (p-1 non-identity elements) form singleton conjugacy classes since they're central. So there are at least p conjugacy classes (p-1 central non-identity singletons + identity + ...). That's way more than 2.

So the Heisenberg group doesn't work. Let me reconsider.

Actually, for a group to have exactly two conjugacy classes, we need: {e} and G\{e}. So the center Z(G) must be trivial (since any central element forms its own conjugacy class, and if there's a non-identity central element, we'd have at least 3 conjugacy classes: {e}, {z}, and the rest).

Wait, unless |G| = 2. If |G| = 2, then G = {e, g}, Z(G) = G, and the conjugacy classes are {e} and {g}. That's exactly two. So Z/2Z works.

For |G| > 2: Z(G) must be trivial. And all non-identity elements must be conjugate.

Now, the class equation: |G| = 1 + |G\{e}| = 1 + (|G| - 1). The conjugacy class of any non-identity element has size |G| - 1. The size of a conjugacy class divides |G| (it equals |G|/|C_G(g)|). So |G| - 1 divides |G|. Since |G| - 1 divides |G| and |G| - 1 divides |G| - 1, it divides gcd(|G|, |G|-1) = 1. So |G| - 1 = 1, meaning |G| = 2.

Wait, that's a clean argument! The size of the conjugacy class of a non-identity element g is |G|/|C_G(g)|, which must divide |G|. But the conjugacy class of g is G\{e}, which has size |G| - 1. So |G| - 1 divides |G|, which forces |G| - 1 = 1, i.e., |G| = 2.

So the only finite group with exactly two conjugacy classes is Z/2Z.

Let me double-check this argument. The conjugacy class of g has size |G : C_G(g)| = |G|/|C_G(g)|. This is an integer dividing |G|. If the conjugacy class is G\{e}, its size is |G| - 1. So |G| - 1 = |G|/|C_G(g)| for some integer |C_G(g)|. This means |G| - 1 divides |G|. Indeed, |G| - 1 | |G| implies |G| - 1 | 1, so |G| = 2.

For |G| = 2, G ≅ Z/2Z, which has conjugacy classes {e} and {g}. ✓

So the answer is: the only finite group with exactly two conjugacy classes is the cyclic group of order 2, Z/2Z.
